text: You have a cleaned dataset, tested code, two answered questions, and a chart. But an analysis nobody understands changes nothing, and a project nobody can find doesn't help your career. This final lesson turns your work into a story a busy stakeholder will actually act on, and a portfolio piece a hiring manager can evaluate in five minutes.

Stakeholders don't want your process — they want your conclusion, then the evidence behind it. A useful structure: a headline, one sentence that answers the question. Evidence, two or three numbers, or one chart, that backs it up. So what, the action this suggests. Caveats, what could make you wrong. And next steps, what you'd do with more time or more data.

Here's how our capstone actually reads. Headline: revenue is concentrated in the North region, in Electronics, and in the fourth quarter, and discounts didn't increase items per order while returns ran higher on discounted orders. Evidence: about 184 thousand dollars from 1,267 completed orders, with Q4 alone at 34.6 percent of revenue, and return rates climbing from 7.2 percent with no discount up to 12.6 percent at 21 to 30 percent off. Caveat: the deepest discount band has only 103 orders, so this is association, not proof of cause. Notice how stating that caveat makes the whole analysis more credible, not less.

Never retype numbers into a report by hand. Compute them once, straight from the cleaned file — read it back in, filter to completed orders, and build a summary dictionary: order count, total revenue, Q4's share, the top region, the top category. On our data that prints 1,267 orders, 183,979 dollars in revenue, North as the top region, Electronics as the top category. Because the raw data is seeded and the whole pipeline is code, rerunning it always reproduces these exact same figures.

A README is the front door of your project — keep it short and scannable. State the question up top: where does revenue come from, and do discounts work. List the key findings in plain bullets. Give exact steps to run it: create a virtual environment, install requirements, generate the data, run the notebook with Restart and Run All. And state your assumptions and limits honestly — quantities kept between 1 and 20, a missing discount treated as zero. Being upfront that the data is illustrative is a genuine strength; hiring managers value clear limits far more than inflated claims.

Before you publish your repository, confirm a short checklist. It runs from scratch — a fresh clone plus your README steps actually reproduces your results. Requirements dot txt and your seeds are in place, from the reproducibility lesson. Your tests pass and cover the key cleaning functions. The notebook is clean — headings, small functions, and Restart and Run All succeeds without errors. There are no secrets or private data anywhere in the repo. And your findings sit right at the top of the README, leading with the answer and a chart.

Practice a five-minute walkthrough: the business question in 30 seconds, what was wrong with the data and how you handled it in one minute, the two findings with the chart in two minutes, and caveats and next steps in the final minute, leaving room for questions. In interviews, describe decisions rather than syntax — why you set a quantity rule at 1 to 20, how you tested it, and what you'd check next with more time.

When you're ready, repeat this whole workflow on a real public dataset — Kaggle, the UCI Machine Learning Repository, or a government open-data portal all work, just check each dataset's license first. A second project proves the method wasn't a one-off. You started this course setting up Python, and you're finishing with a tested, reproducible, end-to-end analysis — you can write Python for data work, use NumPy and pandas fluently, clean messy data, and structure code so others can trust it. The next course in the Data Scientist path is Statistics and Probability for Data Science, which supplies the reasoning behind what we could only flag here — how confident you can really be in a difference like 7.2 percent versus 12.6 percent.
